bibliography.checked_against: Crossref (doi:10.1016/0040-5809(78)90006-0) and the title page ('THEORETICAL POPULATION BIOLOGY 14, 76-104 (1978)')
bibliography.note: Belovsky, G. E. & Jordan, P. A. 1978. The time-energy budget of a moose. Theoretical Population Biology 14(1): 76-104 - matches Crossref (vol. 14, issue 1, pp. 76-104, August 1978). show.mjs reported 'DOI NOT FOUND' only because it cut the DOI at the first parenthesis ('10.1016/0040-5809(78'); the full DOI resolves at Crossref.

claims.claim: on Isle Royale moose fed in water on 108 of 124 summer days
claims.location: p. 93 (PDF p. 18), Table X; the 124-day summer p. 78 (PDF p. 3)
claims.quote: Food removed (kg/pond/summer) 562.7 … Moose density (no./pond) 6 … Days of feeding 108
claims.conditions: Yellow Birch study area pond, summer 1973; 108 is the 'days of feeding' divisor for aquatics in Table X, against 124 days (leaf emergence to leaf fall) for leaves and herbs
claims.note: read on the page image. The paper never explains the 108: it may be the length of the aquatic-feeding season at the pond rather than the share of days on which each moose fed. 'Fed in water on 108 of 124 summer days' is a fair reading; the model's per-day probability AQ_P = 108/124 = 0.87 is an interpretation of it.

claims.conditions: 15 24-hour watches (360 h) from fixed points in forest and at ponds, 194 feeding moose; 'moose appear to be largely nocturnal during the summer'

claims.claim: about half of wet intake (aquatic 17.4 kg wet a day)
claims.conditions: grams wet per day, Yellow Birch Forest, from Table X's dry intakes and the plants' water content (aquatics 95 %)

claims.claim: the pond diet was 58 % stoneworts and 15.5 % Potamogeton (code: water horsetail 9.7, sedges 9.2, spikerush 5.8 %)
claims.quote: Nitella sp. and Chara sp. 11.4 58.4 … Potomegeton sp. 6.8 15.5
claims.conditions: Yellow Birch pond, summer 1973; % of diet by dry weight from the hand-cropping simulations (684.5 g sampled); Carex 9.2, Equisetum fluviatile 9.7, Eleocharis 5.8, other 1.4 %. Coastal pond: Spirogyra 99 %
claims.note: read on the page image. 'Stoneworts' = Nitella and Chara together, as the table lumps them. The composition is that of simulated bites in favoured spots, on the authors' assumption that moose are unselective once submerged.

claims.paper: §3.8.4 (pond area and percentage by project arithmetic)
claims.claim: six moose removed about 17 % of a 2.5-ha beaver pond's aquatic production
claims.source_value: 6 moose (Table X) removed 562.7 kg (Table X) or 580.1 kg (Table II) of a pond production of 3,217.1 kg/summer (Table I) = 17.5-18.0 % of the whole pond's production. But Table I's footnote says only 32 % of the pond is open water and the rest grassy hummock 'twice as productive'; with the open-water rate of 129.03 g/m² that makes the pond ≈ 1.5 ha (3,217.1 kg ÷ 129.03 g/m² ÷ 1.68), not 2.5 ha. Moose fed only in the open water, where they took ~82 % of the growth (Table II: 148.2 g left on 6.3 m² = 23.5 of 129.0 g/m²)
claims.location: p. 79 (PDF p. 4), Table I and footnote b; p. 80 (PDF p. 5), Table II; p. 93 (PDF p. 18), Table X
claims.quote: Our observations indicate that 32% of the pond is open water and the remainder is
claims.conditions: the only pond in the Yellow Birch study area, 1973; production from two 120-m² exclosures (49 quarter-m² clips); removal from 25 clips outside
claims.note: 2.5 ha comes from dividing the pond total by the open-water rate as if the whole pond yielded it (3,217.1 / 0.12903 kg/m² = 2.49 ha), which ignores the footnote attached to that very row. The source's two removal figures differ (580.1 in Table II, 562.7 in Table X). Suggested wording: 'six moose cropped about 80 % of the open water's plant growth, about 17-18 % of the whole pond's production (hummocks included), in a pond of roughly 1.5 ha'. The source calls it 'the only pond in the Yellow Birch study area', with beaver and muskrat present; 'beaver pond' is a fair inference (the lowlands are 'interspersed with beaver ponds') but not stated.

claims.claim: none was seen to defecate in 65 h in ponds
claims.quote: in 65 hours of observing moose in ponds, defecation was never seen
claims.conditions: against frequent defecation in 48 h of watching moose on land; used to justify counting feces only on land

claims.claim: so moose carry aquatic nitrogen and phosphorus to land
claims.note: the source says nothing about nitrogen, phosphorus or nutrient transport; it reports only the 65 h without defecation in ponds (and, p. 102, that aquatic plants are Isle Royale moose's only sodium source, citing Botkin et al. 1973 and Jordan et al. 1973). The N and P transfer is a reasonable inference and should be labelled 'project inference' rather than attributed to Belovsky & Jordan.

notes: Full text (29 pp.) read; Tables I, II, VI, VII, X, XI, XIII and the p. 94 percentages read on the page images (the text layer scrambles them). One correction: the '2.5-ha' pond in §3.8.4 ignores Table I's footnote (32 % open water, hummocks twice as productive) - the pond is ~1.5 ha by that footnote, and moose took ~80 % of the open water's growth, 17-18 % of the whole pond's. One attribution to fix: the N and P transfer to land is the project's inference, not the paper's. Context the rewrite may want: all values are summer (late May-early September) at Isle Royale, Lake Superior, 1972-74; aquatic intake is from one pond in the Yellow Birch area in 1973 (n = 6 moose) and differs sharply at the Coastal pond (161 g/d, Spirogyra); dive time 16.2 ± 8.1 s; aquatics 95 % water (81-99 %), 4.1 kcal/g dry (Boyd 1970, as cited), in vivo digestibility estimated 94 %; total intake 4898 g dry and 33.6 kg wet a day; moose densities 3.1-10.2/km² from feces counts; daily cropping time falls with air temperature (9.43 - 0.29 T h/day, n = 7). The diet percentages come from hand-cropping simulations, not observed bites.
